official_syllabus_verbatim: Social and Political ldeals : Equality, Justice, Liberty.

core_sessions.title: The Ideals Triad: Map, Working Thesis and the Ordering Problem
core_sessions.plain: Equality, liberty and justice answer different questions but must be ordered together in political institutions.
core_sessions.technical: Equality concerns equal moral status and distribution, liberty concerns protected non-interference and agency, and justice supplies the rule for adjudicating their conflicts.
core_sessions.answer: Equality and liberty make rival claims on institutions; justice is architectonic because it decides which liberties are basic and which inequalities are justified.
core_sessions.usage: Define the three ideals separately, expose the conflict between liberty and equality, and use justice to state a qualified institutional ordering.
core_sessions.mechanism: Political institutions allocate status, choice, burdens and benefits; equality and liberty generate claims, and justice ranks or reconciles them.
core_sessions.consequence: A credible answer treats the triad as interdependent without collapsing one ideal into another.
core_sessions.trap: Do not write three disconnected mini-essays or assume that equality means sameness and liberty means licence.
core_sessions.objection: Justice cannot be a neutral referee because rival theories of justice already privilege different liberties and equalities.
core_sessions.reply: The mediation thesis is procedural rather than neutral: it makes the ordering rule explicit and open to public justification.
core_sessions.limit: Do not write that justice mechanically harmonises every conflict; identify the contested criterion and defend a graded ordering.
core_sessions.exam: Define the three ideals separately, expose the conflict between liberty and equality, and use justice to state a qualified institutional ordering.
revision: Equality, liberty and justice answer different questions but must be ordered together in political institutions.
Political institutions allocate status, choice, burdens and benefits; equality and liberty generate claims, and justice ranks or reconciles them.
A credible answer treats the triad as interdependent without collapsing one ideal into another.
Do not write three disconnected mini-essays or assume that equality means sameness and liberty means licence.

core_sessions.title: Equality I: Equal Worth, the Four Forms, Opportunity vs Outcome
core_sessions.plain: Equality begins with equal moral worth but must be specified as legal, political, social or economic equality.
core_sessions.technical: Formal equality removes explicit legal privilege, while substantive equality tests whether social power and conversion conditions make opportunity genuinely usable.
core_sessions.answer: Equality is not identity of condition; it is a demand that relevant differences, unequal opportunities and status hierarchies be publicly justified.
core_sessions.usage: Move from equal worth through the four forms, distinguish formal from fair opportunity, and qualify outcome-sensitive correction.
core_sessions.mechanism: Equal moral worth shifts the burden of proof onto inherited hierarchy; substantive equality then examines access, capability and status.
core_sessions.consequence: Formal equality is necessary but may reproduce disadvantage when starting positions and social power remain unequal.
core_sessions.trap: Do not move from equality before law directly to achieved equality without showing the opportunity and capability mechanism.
core_sessions.objection: Substantive equality can become paternalistic levelling and can underweight responsibility, choice and incentive.
core_sessions.reply: The strongest egalitarian reply targets arbitrary background disadvantage rather than every chosen difference in outcome.
core_sessions.limit: Do not equate equality with identical talents, treatment or final holdings; always state the relevant metric.
core_sessions.exam: Move from equal worth through the four forms, distinguish formal from fair opportunity, and qualify outcome-sensitive correction.
revision: Equality begins with equal moral worth but must be specified as legal, political, social or economic equality.
Equal moral worth shifts the burden of proof onto inherited hierarchy; substantive equality then examines access, capability and status.

core_sessions.title: Equality II: Rousseau, Mill and Marx on Inequality, Individuality and Need
core_sessions.plain: Rousseau, Mill and Marx diagnose different ways in which apparently natural inequality is socially produced.
core_sessions.technical: Rousseau distinguishes natural from moral-political inequality, Mill attacks manufactured female subordination, and Marx shows how formally equal exchange can reproduce class exploitation.
core_sessions.answer: The crucial philosophical move is to ask whether inequality reflects relevant difference or an institution that converts difference into dependence and domination.
core_sessions.usage: Compare each thinker's causal mechanism, then distinguish status equality, individuality and material need before giving a synthesis.
core_sessions.mechanism: Convention, gender hierarchy and class structure transform physical difference or legal equality into social dependence.
core_sessions.consequence: Anti-subordination requires legal status, protected individuality and attention to material structure.
core_sessions.trap: Do not merge Rousseau, Mill and Marx into one egalitarian doctrine; preserve their different mechanisms and remedies.
core_sessions.objection: The three diagnoses rest on incompatible views of property, individuality and the legitimate scope of social transformation.
core_sessions.reply: They can still be compared through one controlled question: how institutions turn difference into hierarchy or dependence.
core_sessions.limit: Do not attribute Marx's higher communist distributive formula to immediate socialism or treat Rousseau's natural differences as political entitlements.
core_sessions.exam: Compare each thinker's causal mechanism, then distinguish status equality, individuality and material need before giving a synthesis.
revision: Rousseau, Mill and Marx diagnose different ways in which apparently natural inequality is socially produced.
Convention, gender hierarchy and class structure transform physical difference or legal equality into social dependence.
Anti-subordination requires legal status, protected individuality and attention to material structure.

core_sessions.title: Equality III: Equality of What? — Sen, Cohen and Dworkin
core_sessions.plain: The equality-of-what debate asks which space—resources, welfare, capabilities or social relations—should be equalised.
core_sessions.technical: Dworkin focuses resources and luck, Sen focuses capability to function, Cohen presses ethos and access to advantage, and relational egalitarians target hierarchy and humiliation.
core_sessions.answer: An equality claim is incomplete until it identifies its metric, its treatment of choice and luck, and the social relation it seeks to transform.
core_sessions.usage: Name the metric, explain its conversion mechanism, test disability and responsibility objections, and compare distributive with relational equality.
core_sessions.mechanism: Resources are converted into real opportunities under unequal personal and social conditions, so identical bundles can yield unequal freedom.
core_sessions.consequence: The chosen metric changes who appears disadvantaged and which remedy counts as egalitarian.
core_sessions.trap: Do not answer equality-of-what with a list of thinkers; compare the metric, conversion rule and residual objection.
core_sessions.objection: No single metric captures need, agency, expensive preference, disability, responsibility and civic standing without loss.
core_sessions.reply: Metric pluralism can retain a primary evaluative space while adding responsibility and anti-humiliation constraints.
core_sessions.limit: Do not cite Sen as advocating equal outcomes; capability evaluates real freedom, not identical functionings.
core_sessions.exam: Name the metric, explain its conversion mechanism, test disability and responsibility objections, and compare distributive with relational equality.
revision: The equality-of-what debate asks which space—resources, welfare, capabilities or social relations—should be equalised.

core_sessions.title: Liberty I: Meaning, Berlin's Two Concepts and Mill's Harm Principle
core_sessions.plain: Liberty concerns both freedom from interference and the conditions of self-direction.
core_sessions.technical: Berlin distinguishes negative from positive liberty, while Mill's harm principle places the burden of proof on coercion aimed at self-regarding conduct.
core_sessions.answer: A liberty answer must identify who is free, from what constraint, to do what, and under whose authority coercion is justified.
core_sessions.usage: Define Berlin's two concepts, apply Mill's harm threshold, distinguish harm from offence, and confront paternalism.
core_sessions.mechanism: Negative liberty protects a sphere against interference; positive liberty asks whether the agent can direct her life; the harm principle tests coercion.
core_sessions.consequence: Liberty requires both a protected domain and disciplined justification of interventions that claim to enable freedom.
core_sessions.trap: Do not treat offence, immorality and harm as interchangeable or ignore Berlin's warning about coercive self-mastery.
core_sessions.objection: Positive liberty can authorise coercion in the name of a supposedly rational or true self.
core_sessions.reply: Enabling conditions can expand agency if they remain rights-bound, contestable and non-perfectionist.
core_sessions.limit: Do not reduce negative liberty to absence of every rule or positive liberty to whatever policy claims to improve welfare.
core_sessions.exam: Define Berlin's two concepts, apply Mill's harm threshold, distinguish harm from offence, and confront paternalism.
revision: Liberty concerns both freedom from interference and the conditions of self-direction.
Negative liberty protects a sphere against interference; positive liberty asks whether the agent can direct her life; the harm principle tests coercion.
Liberty requires both a protected domain and disciplined justification of interventions that claim to enable freedom.

core_sessions.title: Liberty II: Hobbes, Locke, Rousseau, Green and the Equality Relation
core_sessions.plain: Hobbes, Locke, Rousseau and Green connect liberty to different relations between law, consent, security and effective capacity.
core_sessions.technical: Hobbes stresses absence of impediment under order, Locke liberty under known law, Rousseau autonomy through self-legislation, and Green positive capacity for worthwhile action.
core_sessions.answer: Law can restrict particular choices yet constitute liberty when it secures status, consent and the effective conditions of agency.
core_sessions.usage: Compare the thinker's account of law and agency, then test whether enabling conditions protect or paternalistically replace choice.
core_sessions.mechanism: Security, known law, civic authorship and social capability each alter whether formal choice is usable and non-dominating.
core_sessions.consequence: Liberty and equality can complement one another when fair conditions enlarge everyone's effective agency.
core_sessions.trap: Do not present liberty and equality as always zero-sum; identify when redistribution enables rather than suppresses freedom.
core_sessions.objection: Once the state defines worthwhile capacity, positive freedom can erase plural values and personal responsibility.
core_sessions.reply: Green's insight is strongest when enabling provision expands option sets while rights and contestation constrain perfectionism.
core_sessions.limit: Do not call Hobbes a positive-liberty theorist or infer that Rousseau licenses any state command as the general will.
core_sessions.exam: Compare the thinker's account of law and agency, then test whether enabling conditions protect or paternalistically replace choice.

core_sessions.title: Liberty III: Technological Society and Republican Non-Domination
core_sessions.plain: Technological society can expand choice while creating surveillance and platform dependence that expose persons to arbitrary power.
core_sessions.technical: Republican liberty as non-domination distinguishes actual interference from standing subjection to an uncontrolled capacity to interfere.
core_sessions.answer: In technological society, republican non-domination shows why a person may be left alone yet remain unfree when another actor can arbitrarily track, rank, exclude or manipulate her choices.
core_sessions.usage: Separate interference from domination, explain the standing-power mechanism, and test whether law makes technological power contestable.
core_sessions.mechanism: Data concentration and platform control create a standing capacity to shape options even without a discrete act of interference.
core_sessions.consequence: Freedom requires institutional contestability as well as a count of actual interferences.
core_sessions.trap: Do not say non-domination is merely Berlin's negative liberty; its object is uncontrolled status and power.
core_sessions.objection: The domination standard may classify every dependency or unequal capacity as unfreedom and demand excessive regulation.
core_sessions.reply: Republican analysis targets uncontrolled arbitrary power, not all dependence; public rules and effective contestation are decisive.
core_sessions.limit: Do not assume privacy, access or innovation automatically settles liberty; specify the power relation and remedy.
core_sessions.exam: Separate interference from domination, explain the standing-power mechanism, and test whether law makes technological power contestable.
revision: Technological society can expand choice while creating surveillance and platform dependence that expose persons to arbitrary power.
Data concentration and platform control create a standing capacity to shape options even without a discrete act of interference.
Freedom requires institutional contestability as well as a count of actual interferences.

core_sessions.title: Justice I: Procedure, Substance, Classical Forms and Corrective Justice
core_sessions.plain: Justice asks what is due in distribution, correction and institutional order.
core_sessions.technical: Plato treats justice as harmony, Aristotle distinguishes distributive proportion from corrective restoration, and utilitarianism tests institutions by aggregate welfare.
core_sessions.answer: The examiner rewards a justice answer that names the rule of allocation, the relevant criterion and the method of rectifying wrong.
core_sessions.usage: Move from Plato's order to Aristotle's two forms, identify the criteria dispute, and test utilitarian aggregation against separateness of persons.
core_sessions.mechanism: Distributive justice assigns shares by a criterion; corrective justice restores a disturbed equality after wrong.
core_sessions.consequence: Justice requires both prospective allocation and retrospective rectification, with reasons for the chosen criterion.
core_sessions.trap: Do not confuse Aristotle's proportionate equality with equal numerical shares in every context.
core_sessions.objection: Harmony can freeze hierarchy, proportionality leaves the criterion contested, and aggregation can sacrifice minorities.
core_sessions.reply: The traditions remain useful when their allocation, correction and institutional functions are distinguished rather than absolutised.
core_sessions.limit: Do not call every legal decision just or treat corrective justice as a complete theory of distributive shares.
core_sessions.exam: Move from Plato's order to Aristotle's two forms, identify the criteria dispute, and test utilitarian aggregation against separateness of persons.
revision: Justice asks what is due in distribution, correction and institutional order.
Distributive justice assigns shares by a criterion; corrective justice restores a disturbed equality after wrong.

core_sessions.title: Justice II: Rawls, Nozick, Sen, Ambedkar and the Ordering Verdict
core_sessions.plain: Rawls, Nozick, Sen and Ambedkar offer rival standards for judging institutions and realised social relations.
core_sessions.technical: Rawls prioritises equal basic liberties and fair opportunity, Nozick historical entitlement, Sen capabilities and public reasoning, and Ambedkar social democracy grounded in liberty, equality and fraternity.
core_sessions.answer: Modern justice turns on whether fairness is judged by institutional choice, historical entitlement, realised capability or anti-caste social relations.
core_sessions.usage: State each currency of justice, compare patterned and historical views, add capability and fraternity, and conclude with a qualified institutional test.
core_sessions.mechanism: Each theory selects a different informational basis and therefore ranks institutions and inequalities differently.
core_sessions.consequence: The best comparative answer explains why the same distribution can be fair under one theory and unjust under another.
core_sessions.trap: Do not use Ambedkar decoratively; connect fraternity and social democracy to caste-based status inequality.
core_sessions.objection: Each view risks neglecting something central: history, structure, feasibility, responsibility or entrenched status domination.
core_sessions.reply: A layered verdict can protect basic liberties, rectify unjust acquisition, expand capabilities and test fraternity in lived relations.
core_sessions.limit: Do not merge Rawls's difference principle with equal outcome, Nozick with selfishness, or Sen with one fixed capability list.
core_sessions.exam: State each currency of justice, compare patterned and historical views, add capability and fraternity, and conclude with a qualified institutional test.
revision: Rawls, Nozick, Sen and Ambedkar offer rival standards for judging institutions and realised social relations.
Each theory selects a different informational basis and therefore ranks institutions and inequalities differently.

core_sessions.title: Debates, Criticisms, PYQ Traps and Integrated Verdicts
core_sessions.plain: Synthesis requires explicit distinctions, objections and an ordering verdict across equality, liberty and justice.
core_sessions.technical: The triad is reconstructed through metrics of equality, concepts of liberty and rival procedural, distributive, historical, capability and relational theories of justice.
core_sessions.answer: A high-scoring synthesis states the conflict precisely, names the controlling criterion and concedes the strongest residual cost.
core_sessions.usage: Decode the directive, define the relevant ideal, compare named theories, apply one Indian example and close with a defended hierarchy or balance.
core_sessions.mechanism: Definition fixes the evaluative space, comparison exposes conflict, objection tests the rule, and qualification produces the verdict.
core_sessions.consequence: The answer becomes reusable for direct, comparative and critical PYQs without losing doctrinal precision.
core_sessions.trap: Do not substitute quotations or current examples for the philosophical mechanism and the directive's exact demand.
core_sessions.objection: An eclectic synthesis can become an unprincipled list that avoids choosing among incompatible ideals.
core_sessions.reply: A disciplined synthesis states lexical priorities, thresholds or burden-of-proof rules and identifies where trade-offs remain.
core_sessions.limit: Do not end with the slogan that all ideals are equally important; state which claim prevails, under what condition and why.
core_sessions.exam: Decode the directive, define the relevant ideal, compare named theories, apply one Indian example and close with a defended hierarchy or balance.

ascii_panels.title: Printed clause boundary and the ideals triad
lines: OFFICIAL OWNER -> Equality, Justice and Liberty only
EQUALITY asks in what respect persons must count as equals
LIBERTY asks which protected choices and capacities agency requires
JUSTICE asks what is due, by which rule and through which procedure
democracy and citizenship enter only as the 2018 PYQ setting
rights, duties, sovereignty and government retain their later owners
thesis -> distinct ideals, institutionally interdependent

ascii_panels.title: Fourteen PYQs and the executable answer spine
lines: OWNER CORPUS -> 14 verified parts across every year 2018-2025
DEFINE -> strongest sense of the ideal in the stem
DISTINGUISH -> metric, interference, procedure, substance or repair
ARGUE -> claim, named thinker or example, analysis, qualification
COUNTER -> strongest objection and best reply
COMPARE -> run both positions down shared axes
HOW FAR -> state the conditions under which the claim holds and fails
END -> justice orders liberty and equality without replacing either
